marketConclusions: ML implementation, debugging, general coding, project defense, experimental judgment, behavioral stories, and communication are the always-on core.
The job description determines which optional technical material to add. Topics that do not appear in a target role stay outside the weekly workload.
Current Genmo, Pika and Anthropic roles support a bounded unit on visual-model post-training. The public evidence does not support a full course in classical control.
World-model and reconstruction teams expect familiarity with current 3D representations. A role must explicitly require deeper 3D work before that material expands.
No public source provides reliable frequency estimates for generative-vision interview questions, so the plan assigns no numerical probabilities.
limitations: Official job descriptions show work expectations, not exact interview questions.
The strongest broad firsthand account is NLP-centred and is used only for common interview machinery.
Detailed reports of vision interviews are scarce. The domain modules come from current job descriptions and technical claims listed on the CV.
Company processes can change. The 72-hour protocol must use the recruiter's current format description.
taskContract: Every cold test must have a prior source review and supported practice.
Every task names the exact input, timing mode, artifact, stopping rule, and fallback.
Every recurring obligation appears as a rendered checklist item.
One session produces one primary artifact; extra reading is not silently assigned.
A failed gate changes the next task by failure category; it does not expand the syllabus.

pacing.weeknight: Reserve the calendar time shown on the task card. Learning blocks end when the artifact is complete. Gates and simulations use countdowns.
pacing.friday: One brief block: a retrieval pull plus one behavioral rep. Reserve 40 minutes; finishing in 20–35 is normal.
pacing.weekend: Saturday contains two separately reservable blocks with a 15–20 minute break. Sunday is one extended block. Never schedule the blocks back-to-back without the break.
pacing.outreach: One brief block every week from W1 onward. Reserve 40 minutes. One message or follow-up is the completion rule; the clock is not.
pacing.aiOff: All coding tasks are done with AI assistance off. No Copilot, no Claude Code, no autocomplete beyond editor defaults.
pacing.cards: Every knowledge task ends by writing one retrieval card (question / <=40-word answer). Cards are pulled on the Friday of week n+1 and week n+3.
pacing.scopeCut: If a flexible block needs more than its calendar reserve twice, mark the second overrun, stop at the next safe checkpoint, and cut one later Core task using the published cut order. Do not borrow from sleep.
pacing.coreHoursPerWeek: The realistic calendar reservation is about 9h10–12h05 in a full week after adding the Grind 75 sequence. Week 0 reserves about 5h30, slack weeks about 1h30, and Week 15 about 13h because of the full-loop simulation. These numbers include activation, breaks, review, transitions, and overrun buffer.
pacing.totalCoreHours: approximately 114 hours of content work across W0-W15; the default calendar reserve is approximately 154 hours until personal timing data replaces it
pacing.flexRule: Flex is never counted in weekly completion, never rescheduled, never rolled forward.
pacing.backlogRule: A Core task that slips twice is cut, not accumulated, and the cut is recorded.
pacing.learningRule: Use a strictly timed gate only after the assigned source review and at least one guided or open-note practice.
pacing.singleOutcomeRule: One session has one primary artifact. Reading, practice and checking are ordered steps, not separate deadlines.
pacing.timingRule: The task card's calendar reserve is authoritative. Minute splits inside learning-task prose are sequencing hints, not deadlines; the site hides those splits in flexible mode.

timingModel.purpose: The card shows one amount of time to reserve. Use the count-up clock during study. Use a countdown only for a timed interview exercise.

brief.label: Brief
brief.stopRule: Stop when the named artifact is complete; otherwise use the fallback and record the next action.

standard.label: Flexible
standard.rhythm: Two 20–25m focus cycles with a 5–10m break
standard.stopRule: Work the steps in order. At 50m, choose finish, fallback, or one final 15m cycle.

deep.label: Deep
deep.rhythm: Two or three focus cycles with visible breaks
deep.stopRule: Do not compress the reading and artifact into one sprint. Stop at the reserve and save the exact next line.

strict.label: Simulation
strict.rhythm: Countdown for the prompt; count-up for setup and review
strict.stopRule: The prompt limit is real because timing is the skill being rehearsed. Setup and debrief are buffered.

stamina.label: Stamina simulation
stamina.rhythm: Four rounds, protected breaks, food and recovery
stamina.stopRule: Run this session only when rested. Reschedule it if completing it would reduce sleep.

timingModel.briefRule: Friday tasks, outreach tasks, slack-week reviews, and Live retrieval/debrief tasks use the Brief profile unless explicitly overridden.
timingModel.calibration: After three completed tasks, compare your recorded times with the suggested reservation. Increase the reservation when your median is higher. The estimate is there to protect your calendar, not to grade you.
startProtocol: Open only the named source or file.
Write the first artifact heading or function signature.
Start the count-up clock; do not estimate elapsed time in your head.
checkpointProtocol: At 25 minutes: stand or stretch, then choose continue or take the break.
At 50 minutes: finish the artifact, use the fallback, or take one final 15-minute cycle.
At the calendar reserve: stop at a safe checkpoint and write the exact next action.

adaptationRules: Pass a gate -> keep the scheduled mixed-topic coding sequence but do not activate a repair-pool problem. Fail G1 -> replace one later scheduled problem with the matching repair problem; never add it on top of the week. Passing G2 removes extra implementation repair but keeps mocks. Passing G8 removes math repair.
Fail a gate -> the failure category determines the fix, not the topic. See failureCategories.
A real interview outranks everything. Week Core drops to the 72-hour protocol, the Friday pull and outreach. Suspended, not deferred.
Log misses within one hour of every real round. Observed misses take priority over curriculum the following week. Two consecutive misses in one category promote it to a weekend block.
Two consecutive weeks below 70% Core completion trigger a scope cut, not a catch-up.
Slack weeks are recovery, not catch-up, unless Core completion is below 70%.

gates.name: General coding
gates.format: Grind 75 #20 Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters and #21 3Sum after 19 scheduled preparations; unaided, AI off, reasoning narrated
gates.pass: Both correct within the limit; pattern and complexity stated aloud before coding
gates.remediation: Retrieval -> replace one later scheduled problem with the matching repair-pool problem. Time -> repeat one completed Medium with a 25-minute cap. Remediation replaces work; it is never added on top.
gates.retest: W10 using Grind 75 #24 and #25 if failed; otherwise never

gates.name: ML coding
gates.format: Multi-head self-attention from blank after the Week 0 guided adapter walkthrough and Week 1 repair rep; official PyTorch docs only
gates.pass: Output matches the reference on the tiny batch and no narration silence exceeds 20 seconds
gates.remediation: One guided repair of the first broken step, then use the next ML-coding mock as the retest.
gates.retest: W10-T7 if failed; otherwise before each live loop only

gates.name: Debugging
gates.format: Two planted issues in an unfamiliar snippet
gates.pass: Both found by stated hypothesis before any edit
gates.remediation: One extra planted-bug drill per week for two weeks.

gates.name: Vision fundamentals
gates.format: Four retrieval items after a 20-minute source review: conv output/receptive field; weight sharing/equivariance; ViT token/attention shapes; CLIP objective plus one failure mode
gates.remediation: Cards only. Do not re-read CS231n.

gates.name: Breadth retrieval
gates.format: 15 questions across all covered topics, 45 s each
gates.remediation: Missed items enter every Friday pull until answered twice consecutively.

gates.name: Detection and 3D perception
gates.format: Box IoU and greedy NMS from blank; 2x2 Hungarian toy; one 3D point projected through world -> vehicle -> camera -> image; define AP and APH
gates.pass: IoU/NMS match torchvision on a non-tied batch; projection numerically correct; APH defined without notes
gates.remediation: Implementation -> re-code IoU only, timed. Knowledge -> re-read the WOD metrics doc once.

gates.name: Generative image modelling
gates.pass: Four of five items correct, including the CFM target
gates.remediation: Redo the failed derivation cold twice, three days apart.
gates.retest: W11 if failed. If passed, delete all remaining diffusion review tasks.

gates.name: Video and world models
gates.format: 12-minute design of an action-controllable long-horizon model plus five failure modes and one falsifier
gates.pass: Design has shapes, five modes named, falsifier measurable
gates.remediation: Redo the stress-test plan with the decision table written first.

gates.name: RL and post-training
gates.format: Derive the policy gradient; baseline unbiasedness; PPO clipped objective; GRPO in three sentences; one falsifiable held-out reward-hacking test for video post-training
gates.pass: Four of five, including a falsifiable held-out reward test
gates.remediation: Repair only the first broken derivation step or the missing reward-test control, then retest. Do not expand into a general RL curriculum; the six-hour cap holds.

gates.name: Math
gates.format: Three problems covering the material explicitly studied in Week 0: MLP gradient; rank/nullspace/invertibility; expectation/variance/MAP. Pen and paper, no notes. RL mathematics is not included before the RL unit.
gates.pass: Two of three fully correct, with no unstated dimension assumptions
gates.remediation: The single weakest area only, 40 minutes, then re-solve the same problem cold.

gates.name: Training systems
gates.format: 35-minute design with explicit scale assumptions and numbers
gates.pass: Total-compute and wall-clock estimates defensible within 2x; parallelism choice justified against an alternative

gates.name: Inference systems
gates.pass: A cost-per-request number and a named primary bottleneck with justification

gates.name: JAX/TPU
gates.format: Seven definitions closed-book plus a Flax module with a sharded parameter
gates.pass: Six of seven definitions correct; named-sharding example coherent; mesh layout and one host/device failure stated
gates.remediation: Re-read the scaling book JAX chapter once.
gates.retest: Mandatory before any Google, DeepMind, or Waymo loop

gates.name: Research discussion
gates.format: Interviewer picks one of the seven CV lines at random; five-minute pitch plus six adversarial questions
gates.pass: Conceded at least one real limitation, gave a specific falsifier, never used 'that's future work' as an evasion
gates.remediation: Write the missing defense card; re-run with a different random line.

gates.name: Experiment design
gates.format: Ambiguous claim -> design plus five follow-ups
gates.pass: Baseline, confound, metric, decision table and abandonment criterion all present; survived five follow-ups without self-contradiction
gates.remediation: One more design with the decision table written before the design.

gates.name: Behavioral
gates.format: Five unrehearsed prompts, two minutes each, plus one follow-up per prompt
gates.pass: Four of five contain a specific situation, a specific personal action and a specific outcome, within two minutes, no notes
gates.remediation: Retrieval -> missed prompts join the Friday rotation. Communication -> re-record with CDAEI beats timed at 20/30/40/30 seconds.
gates.retest: Before every loop. Do not skip on the grounds that you are well-behaved.

gates.name: Job talk
gates.format: 20 minutes plus 10 minutes of questions to someone who has not seen it
gates.pass: One unifying claim stated in the first two minutes and returned to at the end; every question answered without new slides
gates.remediation: Remove content. Talks improve as plots are removed.
gates.retest: Before any onsite requiring a talk

gates.name: Full-loop stamina
gates.pass: All four completed and round-4 performance no more than one rubric point below round 1
gates.remediation: Longer gaps between real rounds; protect the lunch slot; never book two loops in one week.

protocol.name: 72-hour company-specific protocol
protocol.activation: The moment an interview is scheduled. Replaces the week's curriculum except LIVE-1 (outreach) and LIVE-2 (retrieval).

actions: Collect five inputs (20m): recruiter's words verbatim; role description; two recent papers or engineering posts from the specific team; known format; your own miss log.
Triage to five priorities (25m): score each candidate topic on probability of appearing and cost if fumbled. Hard cap of five. Six means cut the one you would recover from fastest.
Write the one-page brief (15m): role, team, likely scope, three strongest matches, five questions you will ask, three risks, the five priorities. Nothing else gets studied.
Spend 45 minutes rehearsing priorities 1 and 2 aloud. For a paper priority, produce a three-sentence summary and one question for the authors.
Spend 30 minutes completing one live practice round of the most likely interview type without AI assistance.
Spend 15 minutes adapting your research narrative to the team's vocabulary.
Confirm logistics: link, timezone, tool (Colab, CodeSignal, CoderPad), backup contact, charged devices.
Read the one-page brief once. Read nothing new.
Sleep. Liu attributes losing ten minutes to an off-by-one error to two hours of sleep after cramming that never came up.
One shape-trace from memory (transformer block or diffusion step).
Read the five questions you will ask. No new content. Eat.
Record every question asked, verbatim where possible.
Score your performance on the five-axis rubric.
Note interviewer signals: what they pushed on, what they let go.
Write one adjustment for the next round.
Between same-day rounds: water, food, one walk if possible, protect the lunch slot.

weeks.label: Week 0
weeks.theme: Supported foundations: learn first, then measure later

sessions.t: Sat AM · 30m — Coding-pattern refresher: four recognition cues

x.text: On one sheet, make four rows labeled cue / structure / operation cost / first code move. Copy these reminders: (1) contiguous range or substring → array/string indices or a window → one full scan is O(n) → name the left and right indices; (2) repeated membership, counting, or complement lookup → set or hash map → expected O(1) lookup → initialize the set or dictionary; (3) nesting, matching delimiters, or last-in-first-out work → stack → O(1) push and pop → initialize an empty list; (4) merge, reversal, or cycle in nodes → linked-list pointers → O(n) traversal and O(1) local relinking → draw prev/current/next. Cover the right three columns and retrieve them from each cue. If a row is unfamiliar, open only that topic in the Tech Interview Handbook study cheatsheets. Do not solve a problem in this block.
x.why: The first coding question should recall a pattern you have just activated. This block refreshes the selection cues and operation costs used by the first problems without pretending that a trivial warm-up measures readiness.
x.doneWhen: The four-row recognition sheet exists, and you can state the structure, main operation cost, and first code move for all four cues with the right three columns covered.
x.fallback: Write and retrieve only the hash-map and stack rows. Stop after those two rows.
x.repeat: Use the sheet for a two-minute glance before the first three coding blocks, then put it away before opening each prompt.

sessions.t: Sat PM · 55m — Prepare for G2: guided ML coding

x.text: Study (20m): clone CS336 Assignment 1, read the attention and cross-entropy adapter signatures plus their tests, and write the required input/output shapes. Guided practice (30m): implement one adapter with the tests and official PyTorch docs open. Close (5m): run the relevant test and save the first failure. Keep the tests and documentation open during this first implementation; you will attempt the independent version in Week 2.
x.why: The original task demanded two unfamiliar repository adapters under a clock before orientation. Guided contact with the test harness must come first.
x.doneWhen: The shape table exists, one adapter was attempted, and either its test passes or the first failing assertion is saved.
x.fallback: Read the two adapter signatures and write the input/output shapes only.
x.repeat: The actual G2 runs at W2-T2.

sessions.t: Sun AM · 45m — Prepare for G8: math study

x.text: Study (25m): read the definitions and worked examples for expectation/variance in CS229 Probability, then rank, nullspace, and invertibility in CS229 Linear Algebra §§1–3. Guided practice (20m): with the notes open, solve one expectation/variance example and one rank/nullspace example. Do not study or derive policy gradients yet; that belongs to Week 9.
x.why: G8 requires mathematics that has not yet been reviewed. This block teaches those prerequisites before the checkpoint at the end of Week 1.
x.doneWhen: Two worked examples exist and every symbol in them is defined.
x.fallback: Read one worked expectation/variance example and copy it while naming every symbol.
x.repeat: The actual G8 runs at W1-T8.

sessions.t: Sun PM · 40m — Choose starting points and review the CV

x.text: For each of the three preparation blocks, write one line: comfortable, rusty, or new, plus the specific blocker. Do not score yourself or delete future work yet. Then list all seven publication lines on your CV and mark each ready to explain, needs a skim, or needs a full defense pass.
x.scenario: “I see you also worked on X”
x.why: An interviewer may ask about any publication listed on your CV, so every paper needs at least a concise defense.
x.doneWhen: The three starting-point notes and seven publication statuses exist; one focus for Week 1 is circled.
x.fallback: Write the three starting-point notes and circle one focus.

x.text: Write and record a 90-second “tell me about your research” answer with four beats: problem (one sentence), why it matters, key idea, result with a number. Then compress to exactly five sentences of ≤25 words, adding your personal contribution and one honest limitation.
x.scenario: Opening 3 minutes of every research round
x.why: Highest-leverage artifact in the plan; reused in every later defense.
x.doneWhen: Recording is under 90 seconds and the five sentences can be said without reading.
x.fallback: Record one take, no editing.

x.text: Open the blocker you wrote in W0 and choose one response. If coding was the blocker, solve the same Easy problem again with the recognition cue visible. If ML coding was the blocker, finish or repair the same adapter with its tests and the official documentation open. If math was the blocker, redo the same worked example without copying and check the notes after each line.
x.why: Week 0 is now supported preparation, so this task strengthens one named prerequisite before any timed gate.
x.doneWhen: One selected W0 artifact is completed and its remaining blocker is one sentence.
x.fallback: Open the W0 artifact and annotate the first line where you became unsure.

sessions.t: Wed · 45m — CV review: first three paper cards

x.text: Choose the three publication lines marked most important or most exposed in W0. Spend 15 minutes per paper: skim its abstract, main result table, and limitations; then write a three-line card containing the one-sentence claim, strongest objection, and your one-sentence answer. The other four are intentionally deferred.
x.why: Closes the coverage gap found in W0-T4.
x.doneWhen: Three source-grounded cards exist and each can be delivered aloud in under 45 seconds.
x.fallback: Skim and write one card for the most attackable paper.

x.text: Source review (20m): read only the abstract, main figure, strongest result table, and limitations of your strongest first-author paper. Defense (25m): write the three questions you would least want asked, plus one honest sentence toward each.
x.why: Writing the questions you most fear exposes weak evidence and vague ownership claims before an interviewer finds them.
x.doneWhen: Each answer states a real limitation and addresses the question directly.
x.fallback: Write the three questions only.

x.text: List 10 memorable moments: a hard bug, a disagreement resolved with evidence, a pivot, a mentoring win, a production incident, a result you are proud of, a project you killed. One line each.
x.why: Liu attributes her only failed interview to entering a behavioral round without a retrieval-ready story bank.
x.doneWhen: Write 10 moments and include at least three from Lyrebird or Vispera.
x.fallback: Write five.

sessions.t: Any day · 20m — OUTREACH (recurring every week from here)

x.text: Choose the single warmest contact from your Waymo, fal.ai, Adobe, or Amazon network. Spend 10 minutes writing a short message with one genuine update and one concrete request for a 20-minute conversation; spend 5 minutes sending it; spend 5 minutes adding one pipeline row with T+3 and T+7 follow-up dates. One message is enough.
x.why: Relationships and referrals often take months to develop, so outreach must begin before applications open.
x.doneWhen: One message is actually sent and one pipeline row exists.
x.fallback: Draft the message and name the recipient; send it in the next outreach block.

sessions.t: Sat · 2×50m — Five-minute pitch, and career artifacts

x.text: Record a five-minute explanation that covers the motivation, key idea, one numerical result, one limitation, and the next step. Time the recording and mark the section where you ran long.
x.why: A five-minute explanation is long enough to show depth and short enough to reveal unnecessary detail.
x.doneWhen: Recorded and one section marked for removal.
x.fallback: Record three minutes covering motivation and key idea only.

x.text: Send recommendation requests to your advisor, Waymo host, and one external collaborator. Then write a checklist of no more than five later edits to your CV, Google Scholar profile, website, or repositories. Save the actual edits for their scheduled sessions.
x.why: Moved from W14. Requesting letters in mid-November is late; recommenders have their own latency.
x.doneWhen: The three asks are sent and the later-edit checklist has no more than five items.
x.fallback: Send the advisor ask only.

sessions.t: Sun · 60m — G8 math gate, after preparation

x.text: Review (10m): read the two worked examples from W0 and your repaired example from Tuesday. Close the notes. Gate (45m): complete the three explicit problems in G8 math gate. Keep the answer key closed until the timer expires. Close (5m): mark each correct/incorrect and name the first broken step. There is no RL question before the RL unit.
x.why: The earlier study and guided practice make independent recall a fair expectation at this checkpoint.
x.doneWhen: Two of three are fully correct and the first broken step in any miss is named.
x.fallback: Do the linear-algebra problem only, then check it against the notes.

x.text: Expand your strongest project into a one-page map with seven headers, one or two lines each: Problem · Your contribution · Hardest decision · Failed approach · Decisive evidence · Limitation · With 10× resources.
x.why: Kept verbatim. “With 10× resources” is a question Lambert reports being asked directly.
x.doneWhen: All seven filled in language you would say aloud.
x.fallback: Fill Problem, Your contribution, Limitation.

sessions.t: Tue · 45m — G2 ML-coding gate, after preparation

x.text: Review (5m): read the shape table created in W0. Close it. Gate (30m): from a blank file with AI off, implement multi-head self-attention with a causal mask while narrating aloud. Check (10m): compare against F.scaled_dot_product_attention on one tiny batch.
x.why: This timed measurement now follows the W0 guided adapter walkthrough and Week 1 repair instead of appearing cold.
x.doneWhen: Outputs match to ~1e-5 and no silence longer than 20 seconds in the recording.
x.fallback: Write the shape table for Q/K/V through the whole block and stop.
x.repeat: W10-T7 only if G2 fails; otherwise before live loops.

x.text: Trace shape, dtype and device of every tensor through a transformer block for B=2, T=8, D=64, H=4. Write five asserts catching: wrong transpose, head-dim mismatch, mask not broadcasting over heads, fp16/fp32 mismatch, CPU/GPU mismatch. Keep broadcasting rules open.
x.why: Explicit shape, device, and data-type tracking makes tensor bugs easier to localize during live coding.
x.doneWhen: The table is complete and each assert would actually fire on its bug.
x.fallback: Write the five asserts only.

x.text: Answer aloud, ≤7 min each: (1) Why this problem? (2) Why this method over the obvious alternative? (3) Strongest competing approach? (4) What failed? (5) Weakest evidence? (6) What result would falsify your main claim?
x.why: A clear falsifier demonstrates scientific judgment instead of polished presentation alone.
x.doneWhen: All six crisp enough to deliver in an interview.
x.fallback: Answer (5) and (6) only.

x.text: Spend 10 minutes answering three retrieval cards without notes, and record where recall broke. Then spend 15 minutes drafting and recording a CDAEI answer about originating a research direction; keep the recording under two minutes.
x.why: A short weekly retrieval session maintains recall without adding another large study block.
x.doneWhen: You answered the review cards and saved the behavioral response.
x.fallback: Answer the review cards and stop.

x.text: Give the five-minute pitch, and then spend 35 minutes answering adversarial questions from a peer or the prepared list. Include your three scariest questions and the six questions from Thursday.
x.why: Adversarial questioning reveals weak ownership claims and unsupported conclusions that a polished presentation can conceal.
x.doneWhen: At least 12 questions asked and all answered.
x.fallback: Answer your three scariest questions on record.

x.text: Review the recording, identify the three weakest answers, rewrite them, and record those three answers again.
x.why: Revision-after-recording is what converts practice into improvement.
x.doneWhen: You re-recorded both repaired answers.
x.fallback: Identify the three weakest and write one better opening line each.

weeks.label: Week 3
weeks.theme: Debugging, JAX defense, and the first mock

x.text: Open debugging drill 01 without opening the answer key. First five minutes: write two hypotheses without editing. Then run the file, localize both failures, and state a new hypothesis aloud before every edit. Compare with the answer key only after tests pass or the 35-minute cap expires.
x.why: Hypothesis-before-edit is the graded behaviour, not the fix. Expanded from one occurrence to three.
x.doneWhen: Both bugs are localized, and the notes show a hypothesis before each edit.
x.fallback: Read the file, write two hypotheses, and run it once; do not edit.

x.text: Study (20m): read Thinking in JAX through tracing/JIT and run its smallest example. Practice (20m): adapt that example into a Flax nn.Module MLP with an explicit PRNG key and one jit-compiled forward pass. Close (5m): define jit, vmap, and grad; scan is deferred to Week 7.
x.scenario: “Your CV says JAX on TPUs. Walk me through it.”
x.why: The plan’s clearest unforced gap: zero JAX tasks existed across 133.
x.doneWhen: The module runs under jit and you can state why a Python if on a traced value fails.
x.fallback: Run the tracing/JIT example and explain the tracer error in one sentence.

sessions.t: Thu · 45m — Study, then G3 CV-fundamentals check

x.text: Study (20m): review convolution output/receptive-field arithmetic, then ViT Fig. 1 and §§3.1–3.2; use CLIP Fig. 1 and §§2.2–2.3 for the contrastive objective. Close everything. Check (20m): solve one conv output/receptive-field trace; explain weight sharing/equivariance; trace ViT token and attention shapes; state the CLIP objective and one failure mode. Close (5m): make cards only for misses.
x.why: The previous version demanded cold recall without assigning the source review. This keeps the check but teaches the exact material first.
x.doneWhen: Three of four checks are correct; every miss has one retrieval card.
x.fallback: Review ViT Fig. 1 and complete the token/attention shape trace with the paper open.

x.text: Answer three retrieval cards without notes. Then draft and record a CDAEI response about a failed hypothesis and what changed; keep the recording under two minutes.
x.why: The retrieval pull keeps earlier material available, and the story rehearsal prepares one example for behavioral interviews.
x.doneWhen: You answered the review cards and saved the behavioral response.
x.fallback: Answer the review cards and stop.

sessions.t: Sat · 2×50m — First live mock: ML coding

x.text: Keep the check sheet closed, start a 45-minute timer, and open the fixed ML-coding foundation mock. Share the prompt and your screen with a partner, or record yourself if no partner is available. Work without AI assistance and narrate continuously. Stop coding after 35 minutes, and then use the check sheet for 10 minutes.
x.why: Moved from W11. Eleven weeks before the first mock is the plan’s second-largest structural error.
x.doneWhen: The fixed prompt is attempted under timer and all five check-sheet axes are scored.
x.fallback: Open the fixed prompt, narrate the stable log-sum-exp and test plan for 15 minutes, then stop.

x.text: Classify every miss using the nine failure categories, and repair the one with the highest impact. Add its signature to the running checklist for shapes, devices, data types, masking, numerical stability, complexity, and tests.
x.why: Mocks without classified debriefs produce no learning.
x.doneWhen: Repair one miss during the session.
x.fallback: Classify the misses and stop.

x.text: Spend 20 minutes reading Figure 1 and Sections 2.2–2.3 of CLIP. Then spend 25 minutes deriving the symmetric image-to-text and text-to-image cross-entropy for N pairs. Use the final 15 minutes to explain temperature, in-batch false negatives, prompt sensitivity, and the degradation of zero-shot performance under domain shift.
x.why: Contrastive objectives underpin your own CONFORM/CLoRA framing, so this doubles as paper defense.
x.doneWhen: You can write the loss without the paper open.
x.fallback: Write the loss only.

x.text: Spend 15 minutes reading the torchvision NMS contract and the AP/APH description in the Waymo Open Dataset metrics documentation. Then spend 30 minutes calculating IoU for three box pairs, constructing a precision-recall curve from six scored predictions, and explaining AP, class averaging, difficulty levels, heading weighting, and the way aggregate mAP hides long-tail failures.
x.scenario: Defense of the Waymo CV line
x.why: Because your CV names the Waymo Open Dataset explicitly, you need to explain its metrics and their failure modes with precision.
x.doneWhen: You can explain APH and the long-tail masking effect without notes.
x.fallback: Compute the three IoUs and define APH in one sentence.

sessions.t: Tue · 45m — Box IoU and NMS from scratch

x.text: Implementation (30m): write vectorized pairwise box IoU for (N,4), then greedy NMS without torchvision. Tests (15m): run three required cases: identical boxes, disjoint boxes, and zero-area boxes. Compare kept indices with torchvision.ops.nms on one non-tied batch. Nested and tied-score cases are optional after the block.
x.why: One of the few from-scratch implementations worth keeping: vision-specific, fast, plausibly asked of your CV.
x.doneWhen: Kept indices match on the non-tied batch and the three required edge cases behave as documented.
x.fallback: Implement IoU only, with the zero-area test.

sessions.t: Wed · 45m — Detector families and set prediction

x.text: Study (20m): read DETR abstract, Fig. 1, and the set-prediction subsection of §3. Artifact (15m): make a four-row table comparing Faster R-CNN, a one-stage detector, and DETR on assignment, duplicate removal, small-object behavior, and convergence. Practice (10m): solve the assignment for cost matrix [[1,4],[3,2]] by hand and state the total cost.
x.why: The comparison and hand-worked assignment connect detector architecture choices to concrete behavior.
x.doneWhen: The four-row table and Hungarian assignment are correct, and you can explain why DETR needs no NMS.
x.fallback: Read Fig 1 and record a two-minute explanation of why set prediction removes NMS.

sessions.t: Thu · 45m — JAX/Flax CV-claim defense II: sharding

x.text: Study (25m): read the Mesh, NamedSharding, and shard_map examples in How to Scale Your Model, Part 10, running one example if possible. Project map (15m): with the page open, draw the data-parallel mesh you used or would use for the Waymo detector and label the sharded batch dimension. Recall (5m): close the page and define Mesh, NamedSharding, and shard_map.
x.scenario: “How did you actually run this on TPUs?”
x.why: The CV claim needs a concrete, project-specific answer, not vocabulary.
x.doneWhen: You can state the mesh axes and which tensor dimension is sharded on each, aloud.
x.fallback: Define Mesh, shard_map, in_shardings in one line each.

x.text: Answer three retrieval cards without notes, including one card from W4-T1. Then record a CDAEI response about the hardest technical or debugging problem you have faced.
x.why: The retrieval pull keeps earlier material available, and the story rehearsal prepares one example for behavioral interviews.
x.doneWhen: You answered the review cards and saved the behavioral response.
x.fallback: Answer the review cards and stop.

sessions.t: Sat · 2×50m — Camera geometry, then detector architecture

x.text: Write the transformation chain from world coordinates to vehicle coordinates, camera coordinates, and image coordinates. Project one 3D point by hand using the supplied 3×3 intrinsic matrix and extrinsic matrix. List the convention checks that prevent axis-order, handedness, unit, and timestamp-synchronization bugs. Check your work against Section 1 of CS231A Camera Models.
x.why: Narrowed from the old W6 Thu. Multi-view geometry depth is out of scope; one correct projection plus the bug checklist is the interview-relevant residue.
x.doneWhen: The projected pixel coordinate is correct and the checklist is written.
x.fallback: Write the projection equation and the four convention checks.

x.text: Draw a camera-only 3D detector for long-tail and novel objects. Include the image backbone, multi-view fusion, depth or geometry representation, query or proposal layer, open-vocabulary signal, box parameterization, and losses. State every tensor shape at one feature scale. Finish after the architecture because Week 5 covers evaluation.
x.why: Split from the old W6 Sat, which packed architecture and a nine-dimension evaluation plan into 100 minutes.
x.doneWhen: Every arrow has a shape and every component one sentence of justification.
x.fallback: Draw the backbone → fusion → query → head skeleton with no shapes.

x.text: G4 checkpoint (10m): inspect this week’s saved IoU/NMS tests, hand projection, and AP/APH explanation. Record G4 as passed only if all three satisfy its stated criteria. Do not redo them now. Project defense (35m): record a five-minute internship pitch, then answer why camera-only; why this representation; treatment of rare/novel objects; metric choice; what failed; what TPU/JAX changed; weakest evidence. Repair (15m): re-record the two weakest answers.
x.scenario: Any interview that reads your CV
x.why: A specific outcome metric strengthens the most exposed claim in the Waymo project narrative.
x.doneWhen: G4 has an evidence-based result, all seven project questions are answered, and two answers are improved.
x.fallback: Answer ‘why camera-only’ and ‘what stayed weakest’ on record.

x.text: Spend 20 minutes reading Sections 2–3 and Algorithm 2 of DDPM. Then spend 25 minutes writing q(x_t|x_0), the reparameterized noising step, the ε-prediction loss, and the conversions among ε, x₀, and v. Explain the role of the variance schedule and identify one source of numerical error at large t.
x.why: The single most likely derivation you will be asked for.
x.doneWhen: You can reproduce all three parameterization conversions without notes.
x.fallback: Write q(x_t|x_0) and the ε→x₀ conversion only.

x.text: Implementation (30m): write q_sample(x0,t,noise), the ε→x₀ conversion, and one deterministic DDIM-style update using a provided or existing cosine schedule. Tests (15m): check t=0, batched-t broadcasting, and perfect-noise prediction. Dtype/device and final-timestep stress tests are optional follow-ups.
x.why: The most plausible domain-specific ML-coding question for your profile.
x.doneWhen: The three required tests pass and the perfect-prediction case recovers x₀ to numerical tolerance.
x.fallback: Implement q_sample and the t=0 test.

x.text: Study (20m): read Classifier-Free Guidance abstract and the conditional-training/guidance equations in §§2–3. Artifact (25m): derive conditional dropout and the guided prediction, then make a four-row note: quality/diversity tradeoff, oversaturation, batch-doubling cost, and how CONFORM changes the interpretation. Negative prompts and guidance rescaling are optional.
x.why: Connecting the standard object to your own contribution is what makes a research answer land.
x.doneWhen: The CONFORM link is stated as a claim you would defend, not a citation.
x.fallback: Write the guided-prediction equation and the batch-doubling cost.

sessions.t: Thu · 45m — Flow matching, rectified flow, latent geometry

x.text: Study (25m): read Flow Matching abstract, Fig. 1, and the conditional-flow-matching definition in §§2–3. Artifact (20m): compare conditional flow matching and rectified flow on path, target, and solver; then state the geometry assumption relaxed by Aligning Latent Geometry. The scaling paper and likelihood comparison are deferred unless this becomes a company priority.
x.why: Extended to rectified flow at scale, because that is what production generative-media teams ship.
x.doneWhen: You can state the CFM target from memory, complete the three-row comparison, and name the assumption your paper relaxes.
x.fallback: Write the CFM target and one sentence on why straight paths help at low NFE.

x.text: Answer three retrieval cards without notes, including one card from Week 4. Then record a CDAEI response about a research disagreement that you resolved with evidence.
x.why: The retrieval pull keeps earlier material available, and the story rehearsal prepares one example for behavioral interviews.
x.doneWhen: You answered the review cards and saved the behavioral response.

x.why: The second audience provides useful refinement. Cut this task first if the workload is excessive.
x.doneWhen: You removed at least three pieces of jargon and the revised opening was read aloud once.
x.fallback: Rewrite the motivation slide after one read-aloud.

x.text: Deliver 20 minutes plus 10 minutes of questions to at least one person who has not seen it. Score against the rubric.
x.why: Lambert: talks improve as plots are removed.
x.doneWhen: Delivered within 21 minutes and scored.
x.fallback: Deliver the first act only, timed.
x.repeat: Before any onsite with a talk.

weeks.label: Week 14
weeks.theme: Behavioral under pressure and full loops

x.text: Story (25m): turn W13-T4 into one specific responsible-release or research-judgment story with situation, decision, tradeoff, and outcome. Reusable answer (20m): write a four-sentence ‘why this team’ template with blanks for team problem, one recent work item, your matching evidence, and one question. Do not write three company variants now; those belong in each 72-hour protocol.
x.scenario: Values round; closing question in every loop
x.why: The ‘why this lab’ answer is the one every interviewer asks and the one most often generic.
x.doneWhen: One concrete judgment story and one four-sentence fill-in template exist.
x.fallback: Draft the safety story only.

x.text: A partner asks five unrehearsed prompts from the twelve, in random order. Two minutes each, no notes, plus one follow-up each (‘what would you do differently?’, ‘what did the other person think?’).
x.why: Delivering stories to another person tests retrieval, concision, and follow-up handling under realistic pressure.
x.doneWhen: Four of five answered with a specific situation, action, and outcome, within two minutes.
x.fallback: Answer two prompts cold, recorded.
x.prereq: W1-T5 and the weekly story reps

x.text: Complete a full research mock that covers your agenda, one selected project, and one future proposal. Allow the interviewer’s follow-up questions to determine the depth of each section.
x.why: The mock tests whether the agenda, project evidence, and future proposal form one coherent research narrative.
x.doneWhen: Run for at least 40 minutes without notes.
x.fallback: The agenda portion only.

x.text: Complete a breadth discussion covering generative modelling, multimodal learning, interpretability, scale, evaluation, RL, and math. Identify the weakest area and schedule it for Week 15.
x.why: A second rapid-fire discussion tests whether broad knowledge remains accessible under interview pacing.
x.doneWhen: The weakest area is named.
x.fallback: Run the rapid-fire card set instead.

x.text: Answer three retrieval cards without notes. Then record the weakest story from Tuesday’s checkpoint again.
x.why: The retrieval pull keeps earlier material available, and the story rehearsal repairs the weakest example from Tuesday.
x.doneWhen: You answered the review cards and re-recorded the weak story.
x.fallback: Answer the review cards and stop.

x.text: Keep the check sheet closed, start a 45-minute timer, and open ML-coding mock B. Reproduce interview conditions by turning off AI assistance, keeping the camera on, and explaining your reasoning throughout. Stop coding after 35 minutes, and use the check sheet during the final 10 minutes.
x.why: Simulation is the only way to find performance failure modes.
x.doneWhen: Completed without pausing the timer, all five axes scored, and one recovery moment logged.
x.fallback: Open the fixed prompt, narrate the vectorization and test plan for 15 minutes, then stop.

x.text: Complete one research or design round. Track your energy, any loss of communication clarity, repeated mistakes, and your recovery after a difficult moment.
x.why: Recovery after a bad moment is a trainable skill.
x.doneWhen: You logged one recovery moment.
x.fallback: Run 20 minutes.

x.text: Spend 40 minutes repairing the weakness that had the greatest impact during the simulation. Then spend 20 minutes ordering your interviews: schedule practice loops first, high-priority companies second, and dream companies last. Add the next two weeks of interview slots to your calendar.
x.why: Liu recommends practice interviews and warns that stamina is finite. Protect your energy for the companies you care about.
x.doneWhen: Dates exist in the calendar.
x.fallback: Write the company order.

x.text: Build the reusable one-page brief: role, team, likely scope, your three strongest matches, five questions you will ask, three risks. Fill it once for your highest-priority target.
x.why: Becomes step 1 of the 72-hour protocol.
x.doneWhen: The five questions are specific to that team.
x.fallback: Write the five questions.

x.text: One ML implementation or one general-coding problem, alternating week to week. Full block on one.
x.why: The alternating rule is right.
x.doneWhen: One problem completed or deliberately abandoned with a logged reason.
x.fallback: Re-solve a known problem from blank.

x.text: Build one reusable offer-comparison sheet with fields for base, sign-on, equity type and vesting, refresher policy, bonus, relocation, visa sponsorship, and start date. Fill one hypothetical row using a top target’s public band from levels.fyi; compute four-year expected value with one explicit equity-growth assumption. Do not build multiple company sheets before offers exist.
x.why: Liu: initial offers leave room by design and recruiters expect negotiation. Building the model after the offer arrives is too late.
x.doneWhen: Each sheet has an explicit equity assumption written down.
x.fallback: Look up bands for your top two targets.

x.text: Build a one-page rubric: mission alignment, team and manager, technical fit, growth path, compensation expected value, visa and location, deal-breakers. Weight the rows before any offer exists.
x.why: Weighting before offers arrive is the only way to avoid weighting after.
x.doneWhen: Weights are set in advance.
x.fallback: List your three deal-breakers.

x.text: Answer five retrieval cards without notes.
x.why: A short retrieval session checks which material still comes back quickly before active interviewing begins.
x.doneWhen: You answered five review cards without notes.
x.fallback: Answer three review cards and stop.

sessions.t: Sat · 5h30m calendar reserve — G14 full-loop stamina

x.text: Reserve 5h30 on the calendar. Allow 30 minutes to set up and eat, then run four rounds with 15-minute protected breaks: (1) ML coding for 45 minutes, (2) research discussion for 45 minutes, (3) technical breadth or system design for 45 minutes, and (4) behavioral questions for 30 minutes. Leave 30 minutes to debrief and keep the remaining time for transitions or overruns. Drink during every break and log your energy at the start of each round. Reschedule if you cannot begin rested.
x.why: The only gate that tests the thing nothing else does.
x.doneWhen: All four completed on the same day and you can name where performance dropped.
x.fallback: Run two rounds instead of four and mark the gate partial.

sessions.t: Sun · 40m — Transition to the Live Phase

x.text: Confirm your process order. For every currently open high-priority role whose start-date timing fits, submit the application; for target teams without an appropriate opening, create an alert and one dated follow-up instead. From here the numbered curriculum stops and the Live Phase rules take over.
x.why: Delay high-priority applications until the relevant checkpoints are complete. Anthropic, for example, has a 12-month reapplication window.
x.doneWhen: Every suitable currently open priority role has either an application or a documented reason to wait, and the first practice loop is scheduled.
x.fallback: Send one application.

weeks.label: Live Phase (W16 → Spring 2027)
weeks.theme: Active interviewing: follow these rules each week

x.text: Send one new message or one follow-up using the Week 1 outreach process, and update the corresponding pipeline row. Complete this task every week.
x.why: Networking remains the rate-limiting input throughout.
x.doneWhen: One message sent.
x.fallback: Update one pipeline row.

x.text: Answer five retrieval cards without notes every week while you are actively interviewing.
x.why: Retention decays; the cards are cheap.
x.doneWhen: You answered five review cards without notes.
x.fallback: Answer three review cards and stop.

x.text: Solve one problem each week, alternating between ML implementation and general coding. Choose a problem related to a recent miss whenever possible.
x.why: A mistake from a real interview is the most relevant subject for the next coding session.
x.doneWhen: One problem completed or logged as abandoned.
x.fallback: Re-solve a known problem from blank.

x.text: Record every question asked (verbatim where possible), your performance on the five-axis rubric, interviewer signals, and one adjustment for the next round.
x.why: Liu: record notes after the interview; they drive future studying.
x.doneWhen: The four fields are filled.
x.fallback: Write the questions asked.

x.text: Repair the most important miss from the previous interview loop before returning to the scheduled curriculum. If the same failure category appears in two consecutive rounds, assign it a weekend repair session.
x.why: Observed misses are better evidence than any market research.
x.doneWhen: One miss repaired.
x.fallback: Classify the miss.

x.text: Between 72 and 48 hours before the interview, collect the required inputs and select no more than five priorities. Between 48 and 24 hours before the interview, rehearse the two highest priorities aloud, complete one live practice round, and tailor your research narrative. On the final evening, finish logistics by 21:00. On the interview morning, complete one tensor-shape trace and tell one behavioral story without adding new material. After each round, spend 10 minutes recording the questions, your performance, and one adjustment.
x.why: Liu: three days to cram for a slightly different class each time.
x.doneWhen: Five priorities written and nothing outside them studied.
x.fallback: Write the five priorities and the five questions you will ask.

x.text: Within 48 hours of any higher-band offer, send the two-paragraph message: the competing band, your top reason for preferring the recipient, and the specific ask (base / equity / sign-on / start date). Score every live offer against the W15-T4 rubric.
x.why: Liu: initial offers leave room by design; recruiters explicitly invite negotiation.
x.doneWhen: The message is sent within 48 hours.
x.fallback: Score the offer on the rubric.
